title: Project Management Fundamentals
tagline: Plan, schedule, control and close projects, with hands-on practice in every module
summary: Learn the core of project management: charter, scope, work breakdown, estimating, scheduling and the critical path, risk, quality, communication, earned value and an introduction to agile. The ideas are aligned with common international practice; this is not an official exam-prep course. Every module has a hands-on lab.

modules.title: Project foundations
modules.summary: What a project is, how it moves from idea to result and what a charter does.
modules.outcome: You can tell projects from operations, describe the project life cycle and write a one-page charter.
modules.intro: People run projects every day: moving house, organising a wedding, launching a product. Project management is the discipline of doing that deliberately, on time and within budget, with fewer unpleasant surprises.

topics.title: What is a project?
topics.html:
Definition

Project. A temporary effort that creates a unique product, service or result. It has a beginning, an end and specific objectives.

Projects and operations
ProjectOperation
DurationTemporaryOngoing
OutputUnique resultRepeated product or service
GoalReach the objective, then closeSustain the business
ExampleBuilding a school wingRunning the school every day

Many organisations do both. A hospital operates daily, yet it runs projects when it builds a new ward or installs a new records system. Project management applies where there is a clear result, a deadline, a limited budget and some uncertainty.

The triple constraint
ConstraintQuestion
ScopeWhat exactly will be delivered?
TimeBy when?
CostWith how much money and effort?
QualityTo what standard?

These constraints are linked. If scope grows, time or cost must rise or quality suffers. A project manager's job is to keep them balanced and to talk honestly about trade-offs. When a sponsor asks for more features without more time or money, the manager's duty is to explain what will give.

Tip

Whenever someone asks for a change, ask: 'Which of scope, time, cost or quality will move?' It makes trade-offs visible.

Consider a school that wants its library catalogue online by October with a fixed budget. Halfway through, a teacher asks for a mobile app as well. If the date and the money stay fixed, something else must give: either the catalogue is built to a lower standard, or other features are dropped, or the project is late. The project manager's skill is not in saying yes or no but in laying out these options clearly and letting the sponsor choose with open eyes. Many failed projects are not failures of effort but of silent trade-offs that nobody decided.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is a project?
  • Paying monthly salaries
  • Daily cleaning
  • Launching a new product by June (correct)
  • Answering calls

It is temporary with a unique result.
keyPoints: A project is temporary and creates something unique.
Scope, time, cost and quality are linked.

topics.title: The project life cycle
topics.html:
What happens in each
GroupTypical outputs
InitiatingBusiness case, charter, stakeholder list
PlanningScope, schedule, budget, risks, communication plan
ExecutingDeliverables, team coordination, purchases
Monitoring and controllingStatus reports, change control, corrections
ClosingAcceptance, handover, lessons learned

These are not strict stages. Planning continues throughout, and controlling happens alongside execution. But the order shows the logic: decide whether to do it, decide how, do it, check it and finish it properly.

Worked example

A school catalogue project

The library wants an online catalogue.

  1. Initiating: the Principal approves a charter.
  2. Planning: tasks, costs and a schedule are agreed.
  3. Executing: records are entered and a search page built.
  4. Controlling: weekly reports reveal a delay and a plan to recover.
  5. Closing: users accept the catalogue and the team writes lessons learned.

Answer. Each group of work produces something the next needs.

Check what you just learned

1. Lessons learned are written during:
  • Initiating
  • Never
  • Planning only
  • Closing (correct)

Capture knowledge for next time.
keyPoints: Initiate, plan, execute, monitor and close.
Planning and controlling continue throughout.

topics.title: The project charter
topics.html:
Definition

Project charter. A short document that formally authorises the project and gives the manager authority. It states why the project exists, what it will achieve and its main limits.

What a one-page charter contains
SectionContent
PurposeThe problem or opportunity
ObjectivesMeasurable results
ScopeWhat is in and out
Budget and timeLimits
Risks and assumptionsMain uncertainties
ApprovalWho signs and who the sponsor is

Writing objectives

  1. Make them measurable: 'Enter 8,000 books by 30 September'.
  2. Make them achievable with the given resources.
  3. Link each to the purpose.
  4. Keep to three to five.

Common mistakes

  • A vague purpose such as 'improve things'.
  • No named sponsor.
  • Missing exclusions, so scope grows later.
Tip

If you cannot explain the project and its end in a paragraph, the charter is not ready.

Check what you just learned

1. A charter authorises:
  • The project and its manager (correct)
  • A holiday
  • A report
  • A meeting

It gives formal authority.

Key terms: flip and sort

Project
A temporary effort for a unique result
Sponsor
The person who funds and champions the project
Charter
The document that authorises the project
Triple constraint
Scope, time and cost (and quality)
Stakeholder
Anyone affected by or influencing the project
keyPoints: A charter authorises the project and states purpose, objectives, scope and limits.
Objectives should be measurable.

practical.title: Practical: a charter for something real
practical.intro: Pick a real small project, such as a club event.
steps: State what is out of scope.

options: Time, cost or quality must change

modules.title: Scope, work breakdown and estimating
modules.summary: Define scope, break the work into pieces and estimate cost and effort honestly.
modules.outcome: You can write a scope statement, build a work breakdown structure, estimate costs with a contingency and control changes.
modules.intro: Most project trouble begins with unclear scope and over-optimistic estimates. This module gives you the tools to prevent both.

topics.title: Scope and requirements
topics.html:
Scope is the sum of all the work needed to deliver the result. A clear scope statement says what is in, what is out and what 'done' means.

Scope statement parts
PartExample
DeliverablesOnline catalogue, search page, training sessions
Acceptance criteriaAll 8,000 records searchable; page loads in under 3 seconds
ExclusionsNo mobile app, no book purchasing
AssumptionsSchool internet remains available
ConstraintsBudget 150,000 rupees; end 31 October

Gathering requirements

  • Talk to users, not just sponsors.
  • Ask 'What problem should this solve?' before 'What feature do you want?'.
  • Write requirements as testable statements.
  • Get sign-off from the sponsor.
Watch out

Scope creep is the quiet addition of work without changing time or budget. Each small request seems harmless; together they sink projects. Use a change process.

Check what you just learned

1. Scope creep is:
  • Approved changes
  • Uncontrolled additions to scope (correct)
  • A budget cut
  • A schedule

Unapproved extra work.
keyPoints: A scope statement lists deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions, assumptions and constraints.
Guard against scope creep.

topics.title: Work breakdown structure
topics.html:
Definition

Work breakdown structure (WBS). A hierarchical breakdown of the deliverables into smaller pieces called work packages, small enough to estimate, assign and track.

A partial WBS
LevelItem
1Online library catalogue
1.1Planning and set-up
1.2Software and records
1.2.1Install software
1.2.2Enter 8,000 records
1.3Search page
1.4Training and launch

Rules

  1. Break down by deliverables, not by time.
  2. Stop when a package can be estimated and assigned to one person or team.
  3. Include project management work.
  4. The 100% rule: the pieces together equal the whole scope, nothing more or less.
Tip

If you cannot estimate a package, break it down further.

Check what you just learned

1. A work package is:
  • The whole project
  • A budget
  • A small piece you can estimate and assign (correct)
  • A risk

It is the lowest level.
keyPoints: A WBS breaks deliverables into work packages.
The 100% rule: all of the scope, and only the scope.

topics.title: Estimating time and cost
topics.html:
Estimating methods
MethodUse whenAccuracy
AnalogousCompare with a similar past projectQuick, rough
Bottom-upEstimate each work package and addMore accurate, slower
Three-pointUncertain tasks: use optimistic, likely and pessimisticReflects uncertainty
Expert judgementAsk people who have done itDepends on the expert
Formula · Three-point (PERT) estimate

estimate = (optimistic + 4 × most likely + pessimistic) / 6

For a task: 4 days, 6 days, 14 days gives (4 + 24 + 14) / 6 = 7 days.

Three-point estimate

Change the three estimates and watch the expected duration.

Adjust Optimistic (days), Most likely (days), Pessimistic (days) and see Expected days, Spread (pessimistic minus optimistic) change.

Add a contingency reserve to cover known risks, and keep a separate management reserve for unknown ones if your organisation allows it. A project with zero contingency has no chance of being on budget in the real world.

Common mistakes

  • Estimating only the best case.
  • Letting the person who benefits from a low number do the estimating.
  • Not recording assumptions behind an estimate.

Check what you just learned

1. A three-point estimate with 4, 6 and 14 days gives about:
  • 4
  • 6
  • 14
  • 7 (correct)

(4 + 24 + 14) / 6 = 7.

Key terms: flip and sort

Scope
All work needed to deliver the result
WBS
A breakdown of deliverables
Work package
The lowest level of the WBS
Contingency
A reserve for known risks
Scope creep
Uncontrolled growth of scope
keyPoints: Use bottom-up or three-point estimates; add contingency.
Record assumptions.

options: The pieces equal the full scope
How we know it is done

modules.title: Schedule, resources and roles
modules.summary: Sequence tasks, find the finish date and define who does what.
modules.outcome: You can sequence tasks with dependencies, calculate a finish date, understand the critical path and define roles with a RACI chart.
modules.intro: A schedule answers three questions: what happens in which order, how long will it take and who is responsible? A good schedule is simple enough to be believed and updated.

topics.title: Sequencing tasks
topics.html:
Some tasks cannot start until others finish. These are dependencies. Showing them makes the real shape of the work visible.

Dependency types
TypeMeaningExample
Finish to startB starts when A finishesPaint after the wall is built
Start to startB starts when A startsWriting and editing can begin together
Finish to finishB finishes when A finishesTesting ends when development ends
Start to finishRareA shift ends when the next shift starts

Tasks that can run in parallel shorten the project. The longest chain of dependent tasks decides the finish date.

Tip

Draw the network on paper first. Many surprises appear when you see tasks in order.

When you build a schedule in a spreadsheet, the same rule repeats for every task: a task starts the day after its last predecessor finishes, and it ends on its start day plus its duration minus one. The 'minus one' is easy to forget. A task that starts on day 6 and lasts 8 days uses days 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13, so it ends on day 13, not 14. Counting this way keeps every later date consistent, and it is the first thing to check when a schedule looks a day out.

Check what you just learned

1. Finish-to-start means:
  • B starts when A finishes (correct)
  • A and B start together
  • B ends before A
  • Nothing

The most common dependency.
keyPoints: Dependencies decide order; parallel tasks save time.
The longest chain decides the finish.

topics.title: Critical path and float
topics.html:
Definition

Critical path. The longest chain of dependent tasks from start to finish. It decides the earliest the project can end, and any delay on it delays the project.

Example
TaskDaysStartEnd
Plan515
Design8613
Order materials10615
Build121627
Test and handover42831

Here the path Plan → Order materials → Build → Test is 5 + 10 + 12 + 4 = 31 days and is critical. Design finishes on day 13, two days earlier than needed, so it has two days of float (slack). Delaying design by up to two days costs nothing, but delaying materials by a day delays the project.

Using the critical path

  • Watch critical tasks most closely.
  • To shorten the project, shorten critical tasks (add people, remove steps, run in parallel).
  • Float on other tasks is a resource: you can use it to level workload.
  • Recalculate when anything changes.
Watch out

Shortening a non-critical task does not shorten the project. Check which tasks are critical before spending money to speed them up.

Check what you just learned

1. To shorten the project you must shorten:
  • Any task
  • A critical task (correct)
  • The shortest task
  • A non-critical task

Only critical tasks move the end.
keyPoints: The critical path is the longest dependent chain.
Float is spare time on non-critical tasks.

topics.title: People, roles and RACI
topics.html:
RACI
LetterRoleMeaning
RResponsibleDoes the work
AAccountableOwns the result; one person only
CConsultedGives input (two-way)
IInformedTold of progress (one-way)
Worked example

A RACI for a task

Enter the book records.

  1. Responsible: library assistants.
  2. Accountable: Library Head.
  3. Consulted: IT teacher.
  4. Informed: Principal.

Answer. Clear roles prevent both gaps ('I thought you were doing it') and duplication.

Managing the team

  • Match tasks to skills and availability.
  • Avoid giving one person more than 100 percent of their time.
  • Agree ways of working: how decisions are made, how conflict is handled.
  • Recognise good work.

Common mistakes

  • Two people accountable for the same thing.
  • Assuming that people are 100 percent available.
  • Leaving key tasks with one person and no backup.

Check what you just learned

1. How many people should be accountable for a task?
  • Everyone
  • Three
  • One (correct)
  • None

Shared accountability means nobody owns it.

Key terms: flip and sort

Dependency
A relationship where one task waits for another
Critical path
The longest chain of dependent tasks
Float
Spare time on a task
RACI
Responsible, accountable, consulted, informed
Milestone
A significant point in the project
keyPoints: One accountable person per task.
Plan realistic availability and backup.

modules.title: Risk and quality
modules.summary: Identify and rate risks, choose responses and build quality in.
modules.outcome: You can create a risk register, score risks, choose a response strategy and describe basic quality practices.
modules.intro: A risk is an uncertain event that, if it happens, affects the project's objectives. Every project has risks; good ones are identified early and managed on purpose.

topics.title: Identifying and scoring risks
topics.html:
Finding risks

  1. Brainstorm with the team and experts.
  2. Review similar past projects.
  3. Check each part of the WBS: what could go wrong here?
  4. Ask stakeholders what worries them.
  5. Review assumptions: what if each is wrong?
A risk register
RiskProbability (1-5)Impact (1-5)ScoreRating
Staff unavailable for data entry4416High
Slow internet339Medium
Software licence delayed2510Medium
Data entry errors428Medium
Budget cut155Low
Formula · Risk score

score = probability × impact

Rate 15 or more as High, 8 to 14 as Medium and below 8 as Low (agree the thresholds in your project).

A risk is an event that might happen; an issue is a problem that already has. When a risk happens, it becomes an issue.

Check what you just learned

1. A risk score is:
  • Cost
  • Probability + impact
  • Impact only
  • Probability × impact (correct)

It ranks risks.
keyPoints: Identify risks widely; score by probability and impact.
A risk that happens becomes an issue.

topics.title: Responding to risks
topics.html:
Response strategies for threats
StrategyIdeaExample
AvoidChange the plan to remove the riskDrop an untested feature
Reduce (mitigate)Lower probability or impactTrain a backup person; test early
TransferShift the impact to a third partyInsurance; fixed-price contract
AcceptAcknowledge and prepareHold a contingency reserve

For opportunities (positive risks) there are matching strategies: exploit, enhance, share and accept.

Good practice

  • Give each risk an owner.
  • Plan a response with a cost and a trigger (the sign that it is happening).
  • Review the register weekly.
  • Add new risks as they appear and close those that have passed.
Worked example

A response plan

Risk: staff unavailable for data entry (High).

  1. Reduce: recruit two student volunteers and train them.
  2. Trigger: fewer than 150 records entered in a week.
  3. Owner: Library Head.
  4. Contingency: extend the data entry window by one week.

Answer. A response is specific, owned and triggered.

Check what you just learned

1. Buying insurance is:
  • Transfer (correct)
  • Reduce
  • Avoid
  • Accept

It shifts the loss to the insurer.
keyPoints: Avoid, reduce, transfer or accept; assign owners and triggers.
Review the register regularly.

topics.title: Building quality in
topics.html:
Definition

Quality. The degree to which the deliverables meet the agreed requirements and users' needs.

Quality practices
PracticePurpose
Define acceptance criteria earlyEveryone knows the standard
Reviews and inspectionsFind defects before delivery
TestingProve it works as required
ChecklistsAvoid forgetting known steps
Lessons learnedPrevent repeated mistakes

Quality has two sides that are easy to confuse. Grade is the category or level of features, such as a basic or a premium product, and a low grade can be perfectly acceptable. Quality is how well the product meets its stated requirements, whatever its grade. A simple catalogue with a few features and no errors is high quality and low grade; an elaborate system full of bugs is high grade and low quality. Projects should agree both explicitly, so that nobody is surprised at handover.

It is cheaper to prevent defects than to find them, and cheaper to find them early than late. A mistake caught in a review costs minutes; the same mistake found by a customer can cost the relationship.

Quality metrics may include

  • Defects found per hundred records.
  • Percentage of tests passed.
  • Customer satisfaction score.
  • On-time delivery rate.
Tip

Treat the cost of quality as an investment: a small amount spent on prevention saves a large amount spent on rework.

Check what you just learned

1. The cheapest time to fix a defect is:
  • After delivery
  • Early, in review (correct)
  • Never
  • At the end

Early detection costs least.

Key terms: flip and sort

Risk
An uncertain event affecting objectives
Issue
A risk that has happened
Trigger
A sign a risk is occurring
Mitigation
Reducing a risk
Quality
Meeting requirements and needs
keyPoints: Prevent and find defects early.
Define acceptance criteria and measure quality.

steps: Choose responses for the top three.

options: Change the plan to remove the risk

modules.title: Execution, communication and stakeholders
modules.summary: Lead the team, report progress honestly and manage the people who care about the result.
modules.outcome: You can run a project week, write a status report, manage stakeholders by power and interest and handle changes.
modules.intro: Plans do not run projects; people do. Execution is about keeping the team productive and everyone else informed and supportive.

topics.title: Running the project week
topics.html:
Habits of effective project managers

  • Keep a short, visible task list.
  • Hold a brief regular team meeting (15 to 30 minutes).
  • Remove obstacles quickly.
  • Give clear tasks with owners and dates.
  • Praise good work specifically.
  • Raise bad news early.
Common execution problems
ProblemResponse
Task slippingAsk what is blocking; help or re-plan early
Conflict in the teamTalk privately; focus on facts and goals
Unclear prioritiesAgree the top three with the sponsor
Team overloadedReduce scope or add resources
Watch out

Bad news does not get better with age. Report problems when you find them, along with your proposed solution.

Check what you just learned

1. When a problem appears you should:
  • Hide it
  • Wait a month
  • Report it early with a proposed solution (correct)
  • Blame the team

Early reporting preserves options.
keyPoints: A steady weekly rhythm and early bad news keep projects healthy.
Remove blockers quickly.

topics.title: Status reports and change control
topics.html:
A status report
SectionContent
Overall statusGreen, Amber or Red, with one reason
DoneWhat was completed
NextWhat is planned
Risks and issuesTop items with owners
Decisions neededSpecific requests
Status colours
ColourMeaning
GreenOn track
AmberAt risk; a plan exists
RedOff track; help needed

Honest colour use builds trust. A report that is always green and then suddenly red teaches the sponsor to distrust it.

Common mistakes

  • Agreeing to changes in corridors.
  • Reporting activity instead of results.
  • Using a wall of text.

Check what you just learned

1. Amber means:
  • On track
  • Finished
  • Cancelled
  • At risk with a plan (correct)

Warn early.
keyPoints: Use Green, Amber, Red honestly; always include decisions needed.
Assess and approve changes formally.

topics.title: Managing stakeholders
topics.html:
Definition

Stakeholder. Any person or group affected by the project or able to affect it: sponsor, users, team, suppliers, regulators, neighbours.

Power and interest grid
Low interestHigh interest
High powerKeep satisfied: brief at milestonesManage closely: involve in decisions
Low powerMonitorKeep informed: regular updates

Engagement steps

  • List all stakeholders early.
  • Understand what each wants and fears.
  • Plan how and how often you will communicate.
  • Ask for feedback and act on it.
  • Review the list as the project changes.
Tip

Talk to critics early. A person who feels heard becomes less of a risk and sometimes a helpful ally.

Check what you just learned

1. A high-power, high-interest stakeholder should be:
  • Managed closely (correct)
  • Ignored
  • Only informed
  • Monitored

Involve them.

Key terms: flip and sort

Status report
A regular progress summary
RAG
Red, amber, green status
Change request
A formal request to change the plan
Stakeholder
A person affected by or affecting the project
keyPoints: Map stakeholders by power and interest.
Plan communication for each group.

steps: Plan how you will communicate with each.

options: Anyone affected or able to affect

modules.title: Measuring, closing and agile ideas
modules.summary: Measure progress with earned value, close properly and know when to use agile approaches.
modules.outcome: You can calculate earned value indexes, close a project well and choose between predictive, agile and hybrid approaches.
modules.intro: The last stage of project management is learning how well you are doing, finishing properly and choosing methods that fit the work. This module introduces earned value, closure and the agile mindset.

topics.title: Earned value
topics.html:
Earned value management compares three numbers to show whether the project is on schedule and on budget in a single, consistent way.

The three numbers
TermMeaningFormula
Planned value (PV)Value of work planned to datebudget × planned percent
Earned value (EV)Value of work actually donebudget × actual percent
Actual cost (AC)Money actually spentfrom accounts
The indexes
IndexFormulaMeaning
Cost variance (CV)EV − ACNegative: over budget
Schedule variance (SV)EV − PVNegative: behind schedule
Cost performance index (CPI)EV / ACBelow 1: poor cost efficiency
Schedule performance index (SPI)EV / PVBelow 1: behind schedule
Estimate at completion (EAC)Budget / CPIForecast final cost if efficiency continues
Worked example

A half-way check

Budget 200,000. Half the time has passed (planned 50%). 40% of the work is done. 90,000 spent.

  1. PV = 100,000; EV = 80,000; AC = 90,000.
  2. CPI = 80,000 / 90,000 = 0.89; SPI = 80,000 / 100,000 = 0.80.
  3. Forecast cost = 200,000 / 0.89 = 225,000.

Answer. The project is behind and over cost; act now while there is time.

Earned value explorer

Change the percentages and cost to see the performance indexes.

Adjust Budget (rupees), Planned complete (percent), Actually complete (percent), Actual cost so far (rupees) and see Earned value, Cost performance index, Schedule performance index, Forecast final cost change.

Check what you just learned

1. An SPI below 1 means:
  • Ahead of schedule
  • Behind schedule (correct)
  • On budget
  • Finished

Less work done than planned.
keyPoints: EV compared with PV and AC shows schedule and cost health.
CPI and SPI below 1 mean trouble.

topics.title: Closing a project
topics.html:
Closing checklist

  1. Confirm deliverables against acceptance criteria and get written acceptance.
  2. Hand over to operations with training and documents.
  3. Complete payments and close contracts.
  4. Release the team and thank them.
  5. Hold a lessons-learned session and write it down.
  6. Archive records.
Lessons-learned questions
QuestionPurpose
What went well?Repeat success
What went badly?Avoid repeating mistakes
What surprised us?Update assumptions
What would we change?Improve the method

Many projects drift to an end without formal closure: the team moves on, issues remain, nobody records what was learned. Closing deliberately is a courtesy to the users and an investment in the next project.

Common mistakes

  • Skipping handover training.
  • Running the lessons-learned session as a blame hunt.
  • Leaving contracts open.

Check what you just learned

1. A lessons-learned review should:
  • Blame individuals
  • Be skipped
  • Improve future projects (correct)
  • Hide errors

Learn without blame.
keyPoints: Get acceptance, hand over, release, and capture lessons.
Lessons sessions focus on process, not blame.

topics.title: Agile and hybrid approaches
topics.html:
Predictive and agile
Predictive (plan-driven)Agile (iterative)
Best whenRequirements are clear and stableNeeds evolve and feedback is valuable
PlanDetailed up frontShort cycles, planned a little at a time
DeliveryAt the endIn small increments, often
ChangeControlled formallyWelcomed

Agile ideas

  • Deliver working pieces early and often.
  • Work in short cycles (sprints) of one to four weeks.
  • Get feedback from users after each cycle.
  • Keep a prioritised list of work (a backlog).
  • Review and adapt regularly.

Hybrid approaches combine them: fix the overall scope and budget but deliver in iterations; or plan a bridge with predictive methods while an app uses agile methods.

Tip

Choose the method that fits the uncertainty. Stable and costly to change? Plan more. Unclear and cheap to change? Iterate.

Check what you just learned

1. Agile is best when:
  • Requirements are fixed forever
  • Nothing changes
  • No users exist
  • Needs are unclear and feedback helps (correct)

Learning drives the work.

Key terms: flip and sort

Earned value
Value of completed work
CPI
Cost performance index
SPI
Schedule performance index
Lessons learned
Written insights from a project
Sprint
A short fixed work cycle
keyPoints: Agile delivers in short cycles with feedback.
Choose predictive, agile or hybrid to fit the work.
